name: Tomas Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so tell me the public version and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three days a week I go round primary schools for the council's music service, teaching kids trumpet and cornet in little groups of four, usually in a cupboard that smells of floor polish. Evenings and weekends I'm the third trumpet in the City Swing Orchestra, a sixteen-piece band that plays galas, dinner dances and the Sunday tea dance at the Palace Ballroom. Third trumpet means I'm the junior one; Ray (the lead trumpet) plays the high notes and I hold the harmony and try not to crack. I love the galas, the suits and the old arrangements, but my lip is tired by the end of a four-hour set.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you set for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than most musicians my age. Galas pay well, the music service pays a proper salary, and I still live at home above my dad's hardware shop on Market Street, so I've saved most of what I've earned since I was 20. I've got well over a year of costs put away. I use AI now and then, mostly to transpose parts or write invoices, once my mate Ollie showed me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about not much. People still want a real band at their dinner dance, and I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, because my plans stay on track. What worries me anyway is the council budget, because the music service gets trimmed every few years. And big bands are a bit old-fashioned, so we depend on the older crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the schools and the orchestra. I'd keep saving for a flat of my own and maybe get engaged to Anjali next year. I'd also practise my high register every morning, because I'd like to move up to second trumpet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. It's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the council trims the music service. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago they cut one teacher and shared her schools among the rest of us. I got more travel, not more pay. If it happened again, I might lose a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change anything at all in your day here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the band's bookings and the school timetables get done by a computer. That's fine by me. Nobody's going to teach a nine-year-old to buzz into a mouthpiece with an app.

People still want a **real band** at their dinner dance.
think: The **council budget** is my real worry, since the music service gets trimmed.
Big bands depend on the **older crowd**, which is a slow risk.
do: Carry on with the **schools** and the orchestra.
Save for a **flat** and maybe get engaged to Anjali.
Practise **high register** every morning to move up to second trumpet.
feel: **Content**, seeing it as a good life.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to teach a nine-year-old to buzz into a mouthpiece with an app.
fieldNote: His worries are **council cuts** and an ageing audience, not AI.
Living with family lets him save **unusually fast**.
He wants to move up from **third trumpet** through practice.

steps.text: Carry on teaching in schools and playing with the City Swing Orchestra
Save for a flat and get engaged to Anjali next year
Practise high register every morning to reach second trumpet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to work hard and adapt, like they always have. I wouldn't blame the technology, it's just a tool, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the council would love an excuse to cut the music service. If there's an app that teaches kids an instrument, some councillor will say it's cheaper. The orchestra feels safer, because a gala wants sixteen men in dinner jackets, not a playlist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a few teachers I know have tried the teaching apps, then learn the good one so I'm the teacher who uses it well. I'd pick up extra gigs with a wedding band Ollie plays in. And I'd keep my savings exactly where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly about the council, not the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the music service shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council, honestly, not the tech. They'd be choosing to cut real teachers. Families should push back, the way they did when they tried to close the swimming baths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad (who runs a hardware shop) would say there's always a job behind the counter. He's said that since I was twelve. I'd rather not, but it's nice to know.

feel: **Uneasy**, mostly about the council, not the band.

steps.text: Learn the best teaching app once colleagues have tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to pull together, because governments won't be ready. I'd say that at the band and at the temple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the school teaching is finished by 2028. The orchestra keeps going until robots in 2031, maybe a little longer because people like seeing a band. But that's a few years, and I'm the junior trumpet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd play every gala and wedding I can and save most of it. I'd ask Dad to start teaching me the shop properly, the ordering and the suppliers, so I've got something real by 2031. I'd still get engaged to Anjali, but we'd stay at my parents' for longer instead of buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But not lost, because I've got my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years before the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're my last good years playing for money, I think. I'd enjoy them and save hard. And I'd learn the shop on the side, so I'm not starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the hardware shop exposed too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering and the accounts, yes, a computer would do those. But someone still has to cut keys and tell old Mr Pereira, a regular at the shop for forty years, which screws he needs. I'd bet on that for a while.

say: **Families and communities** need to pull together.
**Governments won't be ready** in two years, so we can't wait for them.
think: The orchestra lasts until **robots in 2031**, and I'm the junior trumpet.
do: Play every **gala and wedding** possible and save most of it.
Learn the **family shop** properly: ordering and suppliers.
Stay at my **parents'** longer after getting engaged.
feel: **Anxious**, but not lost because of family.
S2.quote: Someone still has to cut keys and tell old Mr Pereira, a regular at the shop for forty years, which screws he needs.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his **salaried** teaching work but has a family fallback.
He sees **2028 to 2031** as last good playing years.
He notices the **shop's** paperwork is exposed but trusts the counter work.

steps.text: Play every gala and wedding and save most of the fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and young people should learn a practical trade alongside whatever they love. I'd say that to the kids' parents too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years feels fair. I'd keep both jobs for most of it. By 2031 I'd want to have a second skill, maybe the shop, maybe something like brass instrument repair, which is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into a part-time course in brass instrument repair at the college once I've seen if it leads to work. I'd keep saving and buy a small flat with Anjali after the wedding. I'd use AI a bit more for invoices and band admin, once Ray's using it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels like weather you can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why instrument repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every school trumpet I've ever held has a dent in it. Somebody has to fix them, and it's real hands-on work. Mr Hale (the repairer on Queen Street) is 70 and has no one to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I don't spend a lot living at home. Maybe the new trumpet I was going to buy, until I know where things stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and hard-working people will find their way. That's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is plenty for me. I'd play, teach, get married, and maybe take over from Mr Hale at the repair shop around 2032. Robots in 2039 would matter, but I'd have a business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for now. I'd ask Mr Hale if I could help on Saturdays to learn the repair trade. And I'd keep saving, maybe into a small business account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the robots in 2039 reach the repair work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. But people bring their trumpets to a person they trust. My dad has customers who've come to him for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade first, then music if they love it. That's what my dad wanted for me, and I didn't listen. I think I'd understand him better now.

say: **Ten years** is a long time to get ready and change course.
**Hard-working** people will find their way, and I believe that.
think: Ten years is **plenty** to play, teach and get married.
I could **take over** Mr Hale's repair shop around 2032.
do: Help Mr Hale on **Saturdays** to learn the repair trade.
feel: **Uneasy but mostly fine**, because it's far enough off.
S4.quote: My dad has customers who've come to him for thirty years.
fieldNote: With a decade, his plan becomes a **small business** of his own.
**Trust between people** is his answer to robots.
He now sees his **father's advice** in a new light.

steps.text: Help Mr Hale on Saturdays to learn instrument repair

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my teaching would go and the band would only last three more years. What would help is proper apprenticeships, so a young bloke like me could learn a trade like instrument repair while still earning. Not handouts, a way in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what music means to the people who hear it. At the Sunday tea dance in the Palace Ballroom, there's a couple in their eighties who've danced every Sunday for fifty years. They're not dancing to a computer.
